front: Name the six sthānas (points of articulation) and the element each carries.
answer: Kaṇṭha (throat, ākāśa), Tālu (palate, vāyu), Mūrdhan (dome, agni), Danta (teeth, āpas), Oṣṭha (lips, pṛthivī), Nāsikā (nose)

front: Which vowel is kaṇṭhya (throat-born), and why does the first sound of the alphabet live there?
answer: 'a' — the unobstructed birthplace of sound; kaṇṭha corresponds to ākāśa, the space from which all articulation emerges

front: Which vowel and śakti-sibilant are tālavya, and what element is the palate?
answer: 'i / ī' and 'śa'; tālu = vāyu (air) — the first rise of the tongue, the śakti-sibilant present in śiva, śakti, śrī

front: Which semivowel and sibilant are mūrdhanya, and why is this position called the place of transformation?
answer: 'ra' and 'ṣa'; mūrdhan = agni (fire) — the tongue curls to the dome; ra is the fire-letter present in hrīṃ, śrīṃ, krīṃ

front: Which semivowel and sibilant are dantya, and what element does the teeth-position carry?
answer: 'la' and 'sa'; danta = āpas (water) — la grounds (present in klīṃ), sa is the soma-sibilant of satya, soma, sattva

front: Which vowel is oṣṭhya, and why is the lips-position the final gate?
answer: 'u / ū'; oṣṭha = pṛthivī (earth) — the last closure before the sound leaves the body

front: What is Nāsikā, and which two ayogavāha and which class-letters use it?
answer: The nose — used for anusvāra (ṃ) and anunāsika (candrabindu), plus the fifth (nasal) letter of every varga (ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma)

front: Which two vowels are kaṇṭha-tālavya and which two are kaṇṭha-oṣṭhya? Why is this significant?
answer: e, ai (kaṇṭha-tālavya) and o, au (kaṇṭha-oṣṭhya). Their two sthānas fuse into one sound — sandhi made audible in the vowel system itself

front: How many varga (class) consonants are there, and how are they organized?
answer: 25 sparśa consonants, arranged in a 5×5 matrix: five rows by sthāna (kaṇṭha, tālu, mūrdhan, danta, oṣṭha) × five columns by prayatna (aghoṣa, mahāprāṇa, ghoṣa, ghoṣa-mahāprāṇa, anunāsika)

front: Enumerate ka-varga and name their common sthāna.
answer: ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa — all kaṇṭhya

front: Enumerate ca-varga and name their common sthāna.
answer: ca, cha, ja, jha, ña — all tālavya

front: Enumerate ṭa-varga and name their common sthāna.
answer: ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa — all mūrdhanya

front: Enumerate ta-varga and name their common sthāna.
answer: ta, tha, da, dha, na — all dantya

front: Enumerate pa-varga and name their common sthāna.
answer: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma — all oṣṭhya

front: A varga row moves from ka → kha → ga → gha → ṅa. What single arc do all five columns trace?
answer: Seed (unvoiced stop) → seed + breath (aspirated) → life enters (voiced) → full animation (voiced + aspirated) → dissolution into resonance (nasal). From closed seed to open nasal echo.

front: Name the four antaḥstha (semivowel / 'in-between') letters and their sthānas.
answer: ya (tālu), ra (mūrdhan), la (danta), va (dantoṣṭha)

front: Name the four ūṣman (heat/friction) letters and their sthānas.
answer: śa (tālu), ṣa (mūrdhan), sa (danta), ha (kaṇṭha)

front: Name the five ayogavāha and where each is produced.
answer: Visarga (ḥ, kaṇṭhya breath), Anusvāra (ṃ, nāsikā), Anunāsika/candrabindu (nasalized vowel), Jihvāmūlīya (root of tongue, before ka/kha), Upadhmānīya (labial breath, before pa/pha)

front: What are the three vowel lengths and their mātrā counts?
answer: Hrasva (short, 1 mātrā), Dīrgha (long, 2 mātrā), Pluta (protracted, 3 mātrā, chiefly Vedic)

front: Which simple vowels are hrasva and which are dīrgha?
answer: Hrasva: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ. Dīrgha: ā, ī, ū, ṝ (ḷ has no attested dīrgha). The sandhyakṣara e, ai, o, au are always dīrgha (2 mātrā).

front: Name the three Vedic vowel accents and where each lives in pitch.
answer: Udātta (raised — higher pitch), Anudātta (not-raised — lower pitch), Svarita (mixed — a fall from udātta to anudātta within the syllable). Central to Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda recitation; developed in Stage 19 (Svara-Vidyā).

front: Define savarṇa. Which pairs of vowels are savarṇa to each other?
answer: Savarṇa = 'of the same class': identical sthāna and identical ābhyantara-prayatna. Vowel pairs: a↔ā, i↔ī, u↔ū, ṛ↔ṝ, ḷ↔ḹ. This is the condition that fires Savarṇa-dīrgha sandhi.

front: Which vowels are technically termed guṇa, and what makes them the 'middle grade'?
answer: a, e, o. Guṇa is the middle strength-grade of a vowel; e is the guṇa of i/ī, o of u/ū, ar of ṛ/ṝ, al of ḷ.

front: Which vowels are technically termed vṛddhi, and how do they relate to guṇa?
answer: ā, ai, au. Vṛddhi is the strongest grade — one step beyond guṇa. ā strengthens a; ai strengthens e (i/ī-line); au strengthens o (u/ū-line); ār strengthens ar (ṛ-line).

front: Name the two kinds of prayatna (effort) and what each governs.
answer: Ābhyantara (internal) — the manner of contact inside the mouth. Bāhya (external) — voicing and aspiration (śvāsa/nāda, alpaprāṇa/mahāprāṇa).

front: What is spṛṣṭa ābhyantara prayatna and which letters use it?
answer: 'Fully contacted' — the point of articulation is completely touched. Used for the 25 sparśa consonants.

front: What is īṣat-spṛṣṭa and which letters use it?
answer: 'Slightly contacted' — near-contact. Used for the four antaḥstha (ya, ra, la, va).

front: What is īṣat-vivṛta and which letters use it?
answer: 'Slightly open' — a narrow gap that produces friction. Used for the four ūṣman (śa, ṣa, sa, ha).

front: What is vivṛta and which letters use it?
answer: 'Open' — no contact. Used for the svaras (vowels), which flow unobstructed.

front: What is saṃvṛta and which single sound uses it?
answer: 'Tightened / contracted' — a uniquely narrowed vowel effort applied only to the short a in ordinary (laukika) speech. The 'a' in isolation is vivṛta; in words it becomes saṃvṛta.

front: What distinguishes ghoṣa (soft) from aghoṣa (hard) consonants?
answer: The vocal cords vibrate for ghoṣa (voiced) and do not vibrate for aghoṣa (voiceless).

front: Which letters are ghoṣa (soft/voiced)?
answer: The 3rd, 4th, and 5th letters of each varga, plus the antaḥstha (ya, ra, la, va) and ha.

front: Which letters are aghoṣa (hard/voiceless)?
answer: The 1st and 2nd letters of each varga, plus the sibilants śa, ṣa, sa.

front: What is mahāprāṇa, which letters carry it, and what is its exception?
answer: 'Heavy breath' — a strong outflow of air past the point of articulation. The 2nd and 4th of each varga and the four ūṣman. Exception: ha is mahāprāṇa but ghoṣa (soft), which is a commonly tested pair.

front: What is alpaprāṇa and which letters carry it?
answer: 'Light breath' — minimal outward air flow. The 1st, 3rd, and 5th of each varga, plus the four antaḥstha.

front: Every bīja follows one architecture. What are its three components and what does each contribute?
answer: (1) Consonant(s) — the form / sthāna of the energy; (2) Vowel — the life-force (usually ī for śakti-bījas); (3) Anusvāra (ṃ) — the seal, where sound collapses into the point (bindu) and then silence.

front: Dissect krīṃ letter-by-letter (Kālī's bīja).
answer: ka (kaṇṭha, ākāśa) — the first impact of consciousness; ra (mūrdhan, agni) — fire that transforms; ī (tālu) — sustained śakti; ṃ (nāsikā, bindu) — seal into silence.

front: Krīṃ and klīṃ differ by one letter. Which letter, which sthāna-shift, and how does it change the deity?
answer: ra (mūrdhan / agni) → la (danta / āpas). Fire → earth. Krīṃ (Kālī) burns and liberates; klīṃ (Kāma) grounds and attracts. One sthāna-shift, entirely different function.

front: The word 'aham' is said to hold the entire alphabet. How?
answer: a — the first varṇa (first svara); ha — the last consonant (ūṣman, kaṇṭha); ṃ — the bindu where sound dissolves. First → last → seal. Saying 'aham' voices the entire varṇamālā in one syllable.

front: What are the Māheśvara Sūtras and how many are they?
answer: The 14 aphorisms said to have issued from Śiva's ḍamaru at the end of his tāṇḍava; received by Pāṇini as the ordered encoding of every Sanskrit phoneme, and the foundation for pratyāhāra abbreviations.

front: What is an 'it' letter?
answer: The final marker consonant of each Māheśvara Sūtra (ṇ, k, ṅ, c, ṭ, ṇ, m, ñ, ṣ, ś, v, y, r, l). It labels the sūtra but is not counted as a phoneme; it is used only to form pratyāhāras.

front: State the pratyāhāra rule and give the governing sūtra.
answer: 'ādir antyena sahetā' (Pāṇini 1.1.71) — the first sound combined with the last it-marker denotes every phoneme between them (the it itself is excluded). Only forward through the 14 sūtras.
result: denotes all phonemes in between (excluding the it)
example_output: ac = a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, ai, au

front: What does the pratyāhāra 'ac' cover?
answer: All vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, ai, au

front: What does the pratyāhāra 'hal' cover?
answer: All consonants — ha, ya, va, ra, la, ña, ma, ṅa, ṇa, na, jha, bha, gha, ḍha, dha, ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da, kha, pha, cha, ṭha, tha, ca, ṭa, ta, ka, pa, śa, ṣa, sa, ha

front: What does the pratyāhāra 'ik' cover, and what sandhi is it used for?
answer: i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ — the vowels that undergo Yaṇ-sandhi ('iko yaṇ aci', 6.1.77).

front: What do aṇ, ec, and yaṇ cover?
answer: aṇ = a, i, u (the three basic short vowels). ec = e, o, ai, au (all diphthongs). yaṇ = ya, va, ra, la (the four antaḥstha).

front: What do khar and jaś cover, and where do they fire in sandhi?
answer: khar = all voiceless consonants (1st, 2nd of each varga + śa, ṣa, sa) — the environment for chartva and sakārādeśa. jaś = ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da (the 3rd letters) — the ādeśa of jaśtva ('jhalāṃ jaśo'nte', 8.2.39).

front: Define sandhi and give its LEGO reading in this course.
answer: Sandhi (सन्धि) = 'junction'. The phonetic changes that happen when two sounds touch. In the LEGO framing: the 'snap-rules' that transform the joint when two bricks click together.

front: Name the three kinds of kārya (sound change) that a sandhi can perform.
answer: Ādeśa (replacement), Āgama (insertion), Lopa (deletion).

front: Name the three sandhi categories.
answer: Svara (Ac) sandhi — vowel changes; Vyañjana (Hal) sandhi — consonant changes; Viśeṣa / Visarga sandhi — visarga and special cases.

front: Where is sandhi compulsory (nitya) and where optional (vikalpa)?
answer: Compulsory within a word, between an upasarga and a dhātu, and inside a samāsa. Optional between separate padas in a vākya.

front: What is the difference between utsarga and apavāda in Pāṇinian grammar?
answer: Utsarga = the general rule. Apavāda = a specific exception that blocks or overrides the general rule for its narrower scope. When both could apply, apavāda wins where its condition holds; utsarga applies everywhere else.

front: Savarṇadīrgha rule (akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ, 6.1.101).
answer: Two savarṇa (same-class) vowels merge into the long form of that vowel.
result: the long form of that vowel

front: Guṇa sandhi (ādguṇaḥ, 6.1.87): a/ā + i/ī.
answer: → e

front: Guṇa sandhi: a/ā + u/ū.
answer: → o

front: Guṇa sandhi: a/ā + ṛ/ṝ.
answer: → ar

front: Vṛddhi sandhi (vṛddhireci, 6.1.88): a/ā + e/ai.
answer: → ai

front: Vṛddhi sandhi: a/ā + o/au.
answer: → au

front: Yaṇ sandhi (iko yaṇ aci, 6.1.77): i/ī before a dissimilar vowel.
answer: → y

front: Yaṇ sandhi: u/ū before a dissimilar vowel.
answer: → v

front: Yaṇ sandhi: ṛ/ṝ → r; ḷ → l before a dissimilar vowel.
answer: → r / l
condition: ṛ/ṝ + dissimilar vowel; ḷ + dissimilar vowel
symbolic_rule: ṛ/ṝ + dissimilar V → r + V; ḷ + dissimilar V → l + V

front: Ayavāyāva sandhi: e / o before any vowel.
answer: e → ay ; o → av

front: Ayavāyāva sandhi: ai / au before any vowel.
answer: ai → āy ; au → āv
example_input: śrī + ai (via nai) → nāyaka ; nau + ika

front: Pūrvarūpa sandhi (eṅaḥ padāntād ati, 6.1.109): pada-final e/o + a.
answer: → e/o + avagraha (the a is elided)
result: the a is elided; e/o remain, marked by avagraha (')

front: Lopaḥ Śākalyasya (Śākalya's optional elision): pada-final y/v after a/ā + vowel or soft consonant.
answer: The y/v may be optionally elided.
condition: word-final y/v preceded by a/ā, followed by a vowel or soft consonant
symbolic_rule: a/ā + y/v # + V/soft C → a/ā # + V/soft C (optional)

front: Pararūpa sandhi: upasarga ending in a + dhātu beginning with a.
answer: → a (the para form prevails)
condition: upasarga ending a + dhātu beginning a (restricted: aj / edh cases)
symbolic_rule: a + a → a (pararūpa, in restricted upasarga-dhātu contexts)

front: Visarga sandhi: aḥ + a.
answer: → o + avagraha (the following a is elided)
result: aḥ becomes o and the a is elided (pūrvarūpa)

front: Visarga sandhi: aḥ + any voiced consonant.
answer: → o
condition: aḥ + ghoṣa vyañjana (3rd/4th/5th of varga, antaḥstha, or h)
symbolic_rule: aḥ + ghoṣa C → o + ghoṣa C

front: Visarga sandhi: aḥ + any vowel other than a.
answer: The visarga is elided; the a remains.

front: Visarga sandhi: āḥ + vowel or voiced consonant.
answer: The visarga is elided; ā remains.
symbolic_rule: āḥ + V/ghoṣa C → ā + V/ghoṣa C

front: Rephādeśa (visarga → r): (i/ī/u/ū/ṛ/e/ai/o/au)ḥ + voiced sound.
answer: → r
condition: non-(a/ā) vowel + ḥ + vowel or voiced consonant
symbolic_rule: V(non-a/ā) + ḥ + V/voiced C → V + r + V/voiced C

front: Sakārādeśa: ḥ + palatal (c / ch / ś).
answer: visarga → ś (via s → ś by śchutva)

front: Sakārādeśa: ḥ + cerebral (ṭ / ṭh / ṣ).
answer: visarga → ṣ (via s → ṣ by ṣṭutva)

front: Sakārādeśa: ḥ + dental (t / th / s).
answer: visarga → s

front: What is jihvāmūlīya and when does it apply?
answer: A special pronunciation of visarga produced at the root of the tongue, occurring (optionally) before ka / kha. Written with the ardhavisarga sign; in modern practice the visarga is usually left as ḥ.

front: What is upadhmānīya and when does it apply?
answer: A special labial-breath pronunciation of visarga, occurring (optionally) before pa / pha. Shares the ardhavisarga sign with jihvāmūlīya; in modern practice usually written as ḥ.

front: Na-lopa (naḥ prātipadikāntasya, Pāṇini 8.2.7): terminal n of a prātipadika / pada.
answer: → elided
condition: n at the end of a prātipadika (word-base) or pada

front: Ku-tvam (cortolku, Pāṇini 8.2.30): a palatal consonant at word end or before specified suffixes.
answer: → replaced by the corresponding guttural (kavarga letter)
condition: palatal (c-varga) at word end or before certain suffixes
example_input: vāc + [suffix beginning consonant] (as in vāk); pratyañc + t → pratyaṅ + …

front: Jaś-tvam (jhalāṃ jaśo'nte, Pāṇini 8.2.39): a hard (aghoṣa) non-nasal stop at pada-end.
answer: → its corresponding third letter (unaspirated soft)
condition: 1st or 2nd letter of any varga at pada-end
result: → its 3rd (voiced unaspirated) letter of the same varga

front: Anusvāra sandhi (mo'nusvāraḥ, 8.3.23): pada-final m + any consonant.
answer: → anusvāra (ṃ)

front: Parasavarṇa (anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ, 8.4.58): anusvāra + a varga consonant.
answer: → replaced by the fifth (nasal) letter of the following consonant's varga
symbolic_rule: ṃ + varga C → pañcama of that varga + C

front: Śchutva (stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ, 8.4.40): s or ta-varga meets ś or ca-varga.
answer: s → ś; t-varga → the corresponding c-varga letter
condition: s or ta-varga (t/th/d/dh/n) meeting ś or ca-varga (c/ch/j/jh/ñ)

front: Ṣṭutva (ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ, 8.4.41): s or ta-varga meets ṣ or ṭa-varga.
answer: s → ṣ; ta-varga → the corresponding ṭa-varga letter
condition: s or ta-varga meeting ṣ or ṭa-varga

front: Chartva (khari ca, 8.4.55): a non-nasal stop at pada-end before a voiceless (khar) consonant.
answer: → replaced by the 1st letter of its own varga
condition: 3rd/4th letter of varga at pada-end + khar
symbolic_rule: ghoṣa C # + aghoṣa C → aghoṣa (1st) + aghoṣa C

front: Trace 'namaḥ + te' → 'namaste'. Which sandhi fires, and why?
answer: Sakārādeśa (visarga sandhi, dental case): visarga before a dental (t) becomes s. So aḥ + te → as + te → namaste. Sakārādeśa does not need to further transform because the following consonant is already dental s-class.

front: Trace 'mahā + īśvara' → 'maheśvara'. Which sandhi fires, and why does it beat savarṇadīrgha?
answer: Guṇa sandhi (ādguṇaḥ, 6.1.87): a/ā + i/ī → e. Because the vowels are dissimilar (a-class + i-class), savarṇadīrgha does not apply — guṇa is the specific rule for this environment.
